title.en: Tithonus (Alfred, Lord Tennyson) and Death be not Proud (John Donne)

hook.en: Tithonus has lived for ever and begs to die. Donne tells Death it has no reason to be proud. Two poets, two very different attitudes to mortality.

objectives.en: Explain the myth and the dramatic monologue of Tithonus
Follow the argument and structure of Death be not Proud

narration.en: Tithonus has lived for ever and begs to die. Donne tells Death it has no reason to be proud. Two poets, two very different attitudes to mortality.

body.en: In Greek myth Tithonus, a Trojan prince, was loved by Eos (Aurora), goddess of the dawn. She asked the gods to make him immortal, but forgot to ask for eternal youth, so he grows ever older and weaker while she renews herself every morning. In Tennyson's dramatic monologue, the withered Tithonus speaks to the Dawn, contrasting his decay with her beauty and with the mortal men who are lucky enough to die; he begs her to take back the gift and let him return to the earth. Written in blank verse, the poem was begun in grief after the death of Tennyson's friend Arthur Hallam. Read the prescribed text itself; this guide is in our own words and quotes nothing.

points.en: He envies mortals who can die

text.en: Death be not Proud: the argument
1. Death does not really kill: it is only like sleep,
2. Death is a slave to fate, chance, kings and
desperate men; it lives with poison, war and sickness
3. Drugs and charms can bring sleep as well as Death can
4. After one short sleep we wake for ever:

body.en: This Holy Sonnet, one of Donne's religious poems, uses a mixed sonnet form: an octave rhymed ABBAABBA and a sestet rhymed CDDC EE, ending in a couplet. Through apostrophe and personification, the speaker argues like a debater that Death is neither mighty nor dreadful: it is merely a rest like sleep, it depends on other causes, and for the Christian believer it leads to eternal life, after which Death will be no more. The final paradox, that Death shall die, crowns the argument with faith-based confidence. Donne is a metaphysical poet, known for wit, argument and bold conceits.

explanation.en: Tithonus sees death as a lost blessing; Donne sees it as defeated. Both use direct address to a powerful being.

problem.en: Compare the attitude to death in the two poems.

steps.en: In Tithonus, death is a natural release that mortals enjoy and the immortal speaker envies.
In Death be not Proud, death is a weak, overrated enemy that will itself end in eternal life.
Tennyson's tone is mournful and weary; Donne's is confident and argumentative.
Both suggest that endless physical life, or death's apparent power, is not what it seems.

answer.en: Tennyson longs for death as release; Donne defies death through faith; both question our usual fear of it.

heading.en: Too much life, too little death

body.en: Tithonus suffers from too much life; Donne's Death is shown to have too little power. Opposite routes to the same comfort: death is not the worst thing.
